MODEL GUIDE

Dongfeng TE8L and TE8K 6x4 Electric Tractors for Regional Haulage

Use the catalogue row as a starting point, then match the 49 t class tractor to a measured regional route, trailer, charging window and operating reserve.

MODEL GUIDESeptember 29, 20269 min read

TE8L and TE8K configuration at a glance

The project catalogue groups TE8L and TE8K in one row. It lists both as 6x4 electric tractors in the 49 t gross combination weight class, with CATL battery options shown as 400, 466 or 600 kWh, LvKong motor output of 315 kW rated and 510 kW peak, a 4AMT transmission and dual-gun charging at 500–600 A. The row also identifies GB or EU charging by model. Treat those values as family-level screening data rather than a promise that every combination is available on every badge.

Because the published row groups two model names and several options, ask the supplier to identify the exact model code on a signed technical specification. It should state the battery, connector, charging limits, axle configuration, wheelbase, tyres, safety equipment and market version. A family summary is useful for screening, but it cannot settle a vehicle's final mass, payload, legal approval or route capability.

Define what “regional haulage” means for your fleet

Regional work can mean a repeatable warehouse corridor, a collection route with many stops, or a long mixed-duty day with loaded and empty legs. These patterns place different demands on an electric tractor. Start with a representative operating week rather than one ideal trip. Record distance per leg, gross combination mass, trailer type, speed profile, gradients, stop frequency, queue time, shift length and return-to-base timing. Include weekends or seasonal peaks when they materially change dispatch.

For each route, distinguish normal conditions from the demanding but realistic case: a heavier load, a cold start, a detour, congestion or an uphill return. Note where the vehicle waits and whether the wait is predictable. Waiting time can create a charging opportunity only when the truck can safely remain connected, the charger is available and dispatch can tolerate the dwell. Do not assume that a regional tractor will return to the same depot simply because the nominal route map is circular.

Compare the planned trip with the most constraining operational requirement: completing a shift, making a delivery slot, or returning with enough energy for the next assignment. This converts “range” into a fleet question with observable inputs. For detailed selection across tractor classes, consult the Dongfeng TE tractor selection guide; for the separate TE46 4x2 port/short-haul case, see the TE46 route guide.

Choose battery capacity from shift energy, not a headline

The three capacities in the family row are nominal battery choices, not three guaranteed distances. Build an energy record from a comparable vehicle or a supervised pilot. Capture state of charge at dispatch and return, distance, payload or GCW, speed, elevation, ambient conditions, cab climate use and energy consumed by any auxiliary equipment. If the operation includes different route types, keep their records separate rather than averaging them into a number that hides the hardest shift.

Set an explicit reserve for diversions, traffic, weather and charger unavailability. Use the vehicle maker's approved SOC guidance to decide which portion of the nominal capacity is routine working energy. A 600 kWh option may provide more nominal energy than a 400 kWh option, but it can also change cost, mass and charging demand. The fleet should compare those trade-offs against the actual route and approved vehicle limits.

For a practical comparison, model at least a low, expected and demanding shift. Make the assumptions visible: distance, consumption, reserve, charging time and number of dispatches. Do not use a single energy-per-kilometre figure for a route with materially different payloads or terrain. A proper capacity choice is the smallest configuration that meets the operation with an acceptable verified reserve, subject to the supplier confirming availability and market approval.

Design charging around departures and site capacity

The family row's dual-gun current figure does not alone determine charging power or duration. Actual charging depends on the vehicle's voltage and acceptance curve, charger output, state of charge, temperature, current sharing between connectors and site electrical limits. Request a vehicle-specific charging curve or written operating envelope; ask the charger provider to confirm the equipment can deliver the required output under the site's conditions. Avoid converting a current figure directly into a promised charge time.

Map arrival windows, unloading, inspection, driver breaks, overnight parking and the next departure. If several trucks return together, calculate coincident demand instead of sizing each charger in isolation. A staggered dispatch or managed charging schedule may release capacity, but it must be tested against the real timetable. Confirm cable reach, parking orientation, connector access, protection and the process for handling a charger outage.

For a route-led site plan, use the electric tractor charging guide as a companion, while remembering that its 600 kWh examples do not certify this family’s charge time. The final quote should state connector type and market variant explicitly: the TE8K is listed with EU interface availability, but the project row groups charging by model, so verify the exact TE8L or TE8K order.

Check trailer, road and driver interfaces

A 6x4 layout and 49 t GCW reference do not establish the payload or legality of a particular tractor-trailer combination. Compare tractor tare, trailer tare, cargo mass, axle distribution, fifth-wheel loading and applicable road limits. Ask for dimensional drawings and confirm fifth-wheel height, wheelbase, turning path, coupling arrangement and trailer electrical and pneumatic connections. A trailer change can change axle loading and operating energy even when the route is unchanged.

Inspect the route at the vehicle's intended operating mass. Look at yard entrances, tight turns, gradients, road shoulders, low-clearance structures, loading docks and places where the combination may need to reverse. If the work includes unpaved sections or slippery access roads, share those conditions with the vehicle supplier rather than inferring traction from the axle count. Tyre specification, axle ratio, controls, braking and the operating surface all contribute to suitability.

Driver handover also needs planning. Make sure the dispatch process explains charging status, route exceptions, safe parking, energy reserve and whom to call when the vehicle cannot follow the planned duty cycle. Train drivers using the final vehicle and local procedures. A configuration that looks adequate on paper may underperform if route assignments, trailer swaps and charge status are not visible to dispatchers.

Limits and common selection mistakes

Do not treat the 49 t GCW figure as payload, the maximum battery as a range guarantee, or the catalogue current as a fixed charging duration. Do not assume the two family members share every option. Exact connector, component package, legal limits, delivered equipment and service scope must be confirmed for the target market. Public-road operation, vehicle approval, taxes and operator obligations also depend on jurisdiction and vehicle completion; obtain local confirmation before committing to a fleet plan.

A common error is choosing a battery before defining dispatch. Another is comparing vehicles only by peak motor power while overlooking rated output, driveline, tyres, axle loads, charger availability and maintenance support. A third is using average daily kilometres when the peak day determines whether the truck can complete the work. Include the empty return, auxiliary use and waiting time; do not silently remove inconvenient parts of the duty cycle.

Regional tractor buyer checklist

  • Country, road rules, steering side and required approval documents.
  • Exact model code, 49 t combination requirement, trailer type and axle-load calculation.
  • Representative route data: loaded and empty distance, grades, speed, stops, queues and shifts.
  • Battery option, measured energy basis, routine SOC window and agreed reserve.
  • Connector, charger make, vehicle acceptance limits, site supply and charging schedule.
  • Wheelbase, fifth-wheel, tyres, braking/safety equipment, payload and dimensional drawings.
  • Training, maintenance responsibilities, parts availability, diagnostics and escalation contacts.
  • Written price, delivery scope, warranty terms and exclusions in the commercial offer.

Send the same route and trailer information to each supplier so that quotations are comparable. Ask them to mark assumptions, optional equipment and values that remain subject to engineering approval. For a tailored review, share the route, payload, daily distance and charging conditions.

Frequently asked questions

Are TE8L and TE8K both 49 t 6x4 tractors?

The project catalogue presents them together in a 6x4, 49 t GCW row. Confirm the exact vehicle-specific specification and approval.

Which battery should a regional fleet choose?

Use measured energy by shift, reserve, charging access and vehicle approval. The largest pack is not automatically the most economical or operationally appropriate.

Can I use the 500–600 A figure to estimate charge time?

No. A time estimate requires the specific truck and charger limits, charging curve, SOC, temperature and site supply.
